Given a multigraph $\mathbf{G}$ with vertices $v_1, \dotsc, v_\mathbf{v}$, we define the space $\operatorname{VC}$ of \emph{vertex chains}\footnote{The terminology comes from homology theory~\cite{Hatcher:2002ut}, which will be a continuing inspiration for our point of view.} to be the vector space of formal linear combinations $x = x_1 v_1 + \dots + x_\mathbf{v} v_\mathbf{v}$. The vertices form a canonical basis for this space, which is isomorphic to $\mathbb{R}^\mathbf{v}$. 

If $\mathbf{G}$ has edges $e_1, \dotsc, e_\mathbf{e}$, we define the space $\operatorname{EC}$ of \emph{edge chains} to be the vector space of formal linear combinations $w = w_1 e_1 + \dots + w_\mathbf{e} e_\mathbf{e}$. The edges form a canonical basis for this space, which is isomorphic to $\mathbb{R}^\mathbf{e}$.

label: prop:ker and im of bdystar
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:ker and im of bdystar}\ifinner\else\mgp{\raggedright\tiny \ref{prop:ker and im of bdystar} prop:ker and im of bdystar}\ignorespaces\fi\ifinner\else\mgp{\raggedright\tiny \raggedright\tiny \ref{prop:ker and im of bdystar} prop:ker and im of bdystar}\ignorespaces\fi\ifinner\else\mgp{\raggedright\tiny \raggedright\tiny \raggedright\tiny \ref{prop:ker and im of bdystar} prop:ker and im of bdystar}\ignorespaces\fi\ifinner\else\mgp{\raggedright\tiny \raggedright\tiny \raggedright\tiny \raggedright\tiny \ref{prop:ker and im of bdystar} prop:ker and im of bdystar}\ignorespaces\fi
If $\mathbf{G}$ is a connected graph, then 
\begin{align*}
\ker \partial^* &= \{ X \in \operatorname{VP} : X(v_i) = X(v_j) \in \mathbb{R}^d \text{ for all } i,j \in 1, \dotsc, \mathbf{v} \} \\
&= \{ Z \otimes \mathbf{1}_{\mathbf{v} \times 1} : \text{$Z \in \mathbb{R}^d$ is a $d \times 1$ column vector} \} \\
\operatorname{im} \partial^* &= \{ W \in \operatorname{ED} : W(u) = 0 \text{ for all $u \in \ker \partial \subset \operatorname{EC}$} \}.
\end{align*}
As a consequence, $\dim \ker \partial^* = d$ and $\dim \operatorname{im} \partial^* = d(\mathbf{v}-1)$.

title: Proof
body_md: Using Proposition~\ref{prop:annihilator props}, $\ker \partial^*$ is the annihilator $(\operatorname{im} \partial)^0$ of $\operatorname{im} \partial$. In other words, if $X \in \ker \partial^*$, then $0 = X(\partial e_i) = X(\operatorname{head} e_i) - X(\operatorname{tail} e_i)$, so $X(\operatorname{head} e_i) = X(\operatorname{tail} e_i)$. Since $\mathbf{G}$ is connected, this implies that $X(v_i)$ is the same for all vertices $v_i$. Similarly, $\operatorname{im} \partial^* = (\ker \partial)^0$, which completes the proof.

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $\partial^T = \partial^*$ if $d=1$,~Proposition~\ref{prop:ker and im of bdystar} tells us that $\ker \partial^T$ is spanned by the constant chains $\mathbf{1}_{\mathbf{v} \times 1} \in \operatorname{VC}$, which are the image of $\mathbf{1}_{\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{v}} = \mathbf{1}_{\mathbf{v} \times 1} \mathbf{1}_{1 \times \mathbf{v}}$. Since $\ker \partial^T \subset \ker L$, this tells us that $\operatorname{im} \mathbf{1}_{\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{v}} \subset \ker L$. Similarly, if $\partial^T \mathbf{1}_{\mathbf{v} \times 1} = 0$, then $\mathbf{1}_{1 \times \mathbf{v}} \partial = 0$, or $\operatorname{im} L \subset \ker \mathbf{1}_{\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{v}}$. 

But $\operatorname{im} \partial^T = \star \operatorname{im} \partial^* = \star (\ker \partial)^0$ only intersects $\ker \partial$ at the origin. Thus $\ker L = \ker \partial^T$ is one-dimensional. It follows that $\operatorname{im} L$ is $\mathbf{v} - 1$ dimensional. Since $\operatorname{im} \mathbf{1}_{\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{v}}$ is one-dimensional, $\ker \mathbf{1}_{\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{v}}$ is $\mathbf{v} - 1$ dimensional. The result now follows from the inclusions above.

\begin{enumerate}
\item $\dim \operatorname{ID} = d \xi(\mathbf{G})$, where $\xi(\mathbf{G})$ is the cycle rank of $\mathbf{G}$. 
\item If $\ell \in \ker \partial \subset \operatorname{EC}$ is a loop in $\mathbf{G}$, then $W(\ell) = (\operatorname{proj}_{\operatorname{ID}} W)(\ell)$.
\item $W$ is in $\operatorname{im} \partial^*$ and hence $W = \operatorname{disp} X$ for some $X \in \operatorname{VP}$ if and only if the failure to close $W(\ell) = 0$ for all loops $\ell \in \ker \partial$.
\end{enumerate}

title: Proof
body_md:
We note that Lemma~2.5 of~\cite{Fritz2019} observes that $\mu$ has finite first moment $\iff$ there is some $Z_0 \in \operatorname{ED}$ so that the $\operatorname{\mathcal{E}}_{\mu}\! \left(\left\| Z-Z_0 \right\|\right)$ is finite. Our decay condition on $p(Z)$ implies this for $Z_0 = 0$, and also implies that the total mass $\operatorname{\mathcal{E}}_{\mu}\! \left(1\right)$ is finite. Of course, any measure with a continuous density with respect to Lebesgue measure is Radon.

Theorem 8.1 of~\cite{Tjur1975} does almost all the work here (recalling that $\operatorname{proj}_{\operatorname{ID}}$ is an orthogonal projection, so its normal Jacobian is constant and one); the only thing we have to prove is that $m_W$ is a continuous, positive function of $W$. 

We note that for any $W \in U$, there is some open $\operatorname{proj}_{\operatorname{ID}}^{-1}(W) \cap U'$ where $p(Z) > 0$. Therefore, the integral $m_W$ of the (everywhere non-negative) $p(Z)$ over $\operatorname{proj}_{\operatorname{ID}}^{-1}(W)$ is positive.

We now show continuity. Suppose we have $W_i \rightarrow W$ in $\operatorname{ID}$. The subspaces $\operatorname{proj}_{\operatorname{ID}}^{-1}(W_i)$ are all in the form $\operatorname{im} \partial^* \oplus W_i$. For each $Z \in \operatorname{im} \partial^*$, we can define $q_i(Z) := p(W_i + Z)$ and $q(Z) := p(W + Z)$. Now
\begin{equation*}
m_{W_i} = \int_{Z \in \operatorname{proj}_{\operatorname{ID}}^{-1}(W_i)} p(Z) \operatorname{\mathcal{H}}^{d(\mathbf{v}-1)}{dZ} = \int_{Z \in \operatorname{im} \partial^*} q_i(Z) \operatorname{\mathcal{H}}^{d(\mathbf{v}-1)}{dZ}.
\end{equation*}

Since $p$ is continuous on $\operatorname{ED}$ and $W_i \rightarrow W$, we have $q_i(Z) \rightarrow q(Z)$ pointwise. By the Lebesgue dominated convergence theorem, to show that the integrals $m_{W_i} \rightarrow m_W$ it now suffices to show that the $q_i$ are dominated by some integrable function $g$ on $\operatorname{im}\partial^*$. 

Since the $q_i$ are shifts of the continuous function $p$ by $W_i$ which lie in a bounded subset of $\operatorname{ED}$ (because the $W_i$ converge), we may assume that the $q_i$ are uniformly bounded on any compact subset of $\operatorname{im}\partial^*$. By the same logic, since $p(Z)/\left\| Z \right\|^n \rightarrow 0$ as $\left\| Z \right\| \rightarrow \infty$ for any $n$, we may assume for any $n$ that there is a single ball $B_n \subset \operatorname{im}\partial^*$ so that $q_i(Z) < \left\| Z \right\|^n$ for $Z$ outside $B_n$. 

We've already argued that there is some $C_n > q_i$ on $B_n$, so we can now construct a function $g_n(Z)$ equal to $C_n$ inside $B_n$ and $\left\| Z \right\|^n$ outside $B_n$ and observe that $g_n > q_i$. If we take $n < 0$ so that $\lvertn\rvert$ is sufficiently large, $g_n$ will be integrable on $\operatorname{im} \partial^*$ (that is, $\int_{\operatorname{im} \partial^*} g_n(Z) \operatorname{\mathcal{H}}^{d(\mathbf{v}-1)}{dZ} < \infty$), completing the proof.

label: defn:decomposition
title: Proof
body_md:
Proving this requires us to introduce Tjur's idea of a~\emph{decomposition} of a measure with respect to a map, which is like a disintegration~(cf.\, \cite{Chang1997}) but somewhat stronger:
\begin{definition}[{\cite[Definition 6.1]{Tjur1975}}]\label{defn:decomposition}\ifinner\else\mgp{\raggedright\tiny \ref{defn:decomposition} defn:decomposition}\ignorespaces\fi\ifinner\else\mgp{\raggedright\tiny \raggedright\tiny \ref{defn:decomposition} defn:decomposition}\ignorespaces\fi\ifinner\else\mgp{\raggedright\tiny \raggedright\tiny \raggedright\tiny \ref{defn:decomposition} defn:decomposition}\ignorespaces\fi\ifinner\else\mgp{\raggedright\tiny \raggedright\tiny \raggedright\tiny \raggedright\tiny \ref{defn:decomposition} defn:decomposition}\ignorespaces\fi
Let $t \colon X \rightarrow Y$ be a continuous function and $\lambda$ be a measure on $X$. A family $\lambda_y$ (for $y \in Y$) and a measure $\lambda'$ on $Y$ are called a~\emph{decomposition of $\lambda$ with respect to $t$} if 
\begin{enumerate}
\item The mapping $y \mapsto \lambda_y$ is continuous (in the weak$^*$ topology on measures),
\item Each $\lambda_y$ is concentrated on $t^{-1}(y)$.
\item For any $f \in \mathcal{K}(X)$, $\int \lambda_y(f) \lambda'(dy) = \lambda(f)$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition}
Conditional distributions are connected to decompositions very tightly by the following:
\begin{theorem}[{\cite[Theorem 7.1]{Tjur1975}}]\label{thm:decomposition and existence}\ifinner\else\mgp{\raggedright\tiny \ref{thm:decomposition and existence} thm:decomposition and existence}\ignorespaces\fi\ifinner\else\mgp{\raggedright\tiny \raggedright\tiny \ref{thm:decomposition and existence} thm:decomposition and existence}\ignorespaces\fi\ifinner\else\mgp{\raggedright\tiny \raggedright\tiny \raggedright\tiny \ref{thm:decomposition and existence} thm:decomposition and existence}\ignorespaces\fi\ifinner\else\mgp{\raggedright\tiny \raggedright\tiny \raggedright\tiny \raggedright\tiny \ref{thm:decomposition and existence} thm:decomposition and existence}\ignorespaces\fi
Let $X \subset \mathbb{R}^m$ and $Y \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ be open sets, $t \colon X \rightarrow Y$ be a continuous map, and $\mu$ be a probability measure on $X$. Suppose that $\lambda_y$ ($y \in Y$) is a family of probability measures on $X$. A set of $\lambda_y$ and $t_\sharp \mu$ are a decomposition of $\mu$ with respect to $t$ $\iff$ the conditional distribution $\mu^y$ is defined for all $y \in Y$ and $\mu^y = \lambda_y$.
\end{theorem}
By~Theorem~\ref{thm:decomposition and existence}, $\mu$ is compatible with $\mathbf{G}$ $\iff$ the $\mu^W_{\mathbf{G}}$ and $\mu_{\operatorname{ID}}$ are a decomposition of $\mu$ with respect to $\operatorname{proj}_{\operatorname{ID}}$. This implies first that each $\mu^W_{\mathbf{G}}$ is concentrated on $\operatorname{proj}_{\operatorname{ID}}^{-1}(W)$. 

Because $\mu$ is $\mathbf{G}$-compatible, it is admissible, and therefore $O(d)$-invariant: for any $Q \in O(d)$, $Q_\sharp \mu = \mu$. We now show that this implies that $Q_\sharp \mu_{\operatorname{ID}} = \mu_{\operatorname{ID}}$.
The action of $Q$ on $\operatorname{ED}$ is multiplication by the $d\mathbf{e} \times d\mathbf{e}$ matrix $Q \otimes I_{\mathbf{e}}$. As a matrix, $\operatorname{proj}_{\operatorname{ID}} = I - \partial^* \partial^{*+} = I_d \otimes (I_\mathbf{e} - \partial^{T} \partial^{T+})$. It follows that 
\begin{equation*}
Q \operatorname{proj}_{\operatorname{ID}} 
= (Q \otimes I_{\mathbf{e}})(I_\mathbf{e} - \partial^{T} \partial^{T+}) 
= Q \otimes (I_\mathbf{e} - \partial^{T} \partial^{T+}) 
= (I_d \otimes (I_\mathbf{e} - \partial^{T} \partial^{T+}))(Q \otimes I_{\mathbf{e}}) 
= \operatorname{proj}_{\operatorname{ID}} Q.
\end{equation*}
where we used Lemma~\ref{lem:mixed product} in the middle steps. Now we know that 
\begin{equation*}
Q_\sharp \mu_{\operatorname{ID}} = Q_\sharp (\operatorname{proj}_{\operatorname{ID}})_\sharp \mu = (\operatorname{proj}_{\operatorname{ID}})_\sharp Q_\sharp \mu = (\operatorname{proj}_{\operatorname{ID}})_\sharp \mu = \mu_{\operatorname{ID}}.
\end{equation*}
We now prove $\mu^W_{\mathbf{G}} = Q_\sharp \mu^W_{\mathbf{G}}$, following the lines of Example 7 in~\cite{Chang1997}. Fix some $Q \in O(d)$. By~Theorem~\ref{thm:decomposition and existence}, it suffices to show that $\mu^{Q(W)}_{\mathbf{G}}$ and $Q_\sharp \mu^W_{\mathbf{G}}$ are both decompositions of $\mu$ with respect to $Q^{-1} \circ \operatorname{proj}_{\operatorname{ID}}$.

We start with the $\mu^{Q(W)}_{\mathbf{G}}$. We already know that $W \mapsto \mu^W_{\mathbf{G}}$ is (weak$^*$) continuous in $W$, so $Q(W) \mapsto \mu^{Q(W)}_{\mathbf{G}}$ is as well. Since $W \mapsto Q(W)$ is also continuous, the composition $W \mapsto \mu^{Q(W)}_{\mathbf{G}}$ is continuous. 

Since each of the measures $\mu^W_{\mathbf{G}}$ is concentrated on $\operatorname{proj}_{\operatorname{ID}}^{-1}(W)$, the measure $\mu^{Q(W)}_{\mathbf{G}}$ is concentrated on $\operatorname{proj}_{\operatorname{ID}}^{-1}(Q(W)) = (Q^{-1} \circ \operatorname{proj}_{\operatorname{ID}})^{-1}(W)$. 

Now suppose we have some $f \in \mathcal{K}(\operatorname{ED})$. We have
\begin{align*}
\int_{\operatorname{ED}} f(Z) \mu(dZ) &= \int_{U} \mu^W_{\mathbf{G}}(f) \, \mu_{\operatorname{ID}}(dW) = \int_{U} \mu^W_{\mathbf{G}}(f) \, Q_\sharp \mu_{\operatorname{ID}}(dW) = \int_{U} \mu^{Q(W)}_{\mathbf{G}}(f) \, \mu_{\operatorname{ID}}(dW).
\end{align*}
We have now established that the $\mu^{Q(W)}_{\mathbf{G}}$ are a $Q^{-1} \circ \operatorname{proj}_{\operatorname{ID}}$-decomposition of $\mu$. 

We now show the same for the $Q_\sharp \mu^W_{\mathbf{G}}$, but it will help to prove this as a Lemma about decompositions in general, because we'll repeat similar arguments later.
\begin{lemma}\label{lem:decompositions push forward}\ifinner\else\mgp{\raggedright\tiny \ref{lem:decompositions push forward} lem:decompositions push forward}\ignorespaces\fi\ifinner\else\mgp{\raggedright\tiny \raggedright\tiny \ref{lem:decompositions push forward} lem:decompositions push forward}\ignorespaces\fi\ifinner\else\mgp{\raggedright\tiny \raggedright\tiny \raggedright\tiny \ref{lem:decompositions push forward} lem:decompositions push forward}\ignorespaces\fi\ifinner\else\mgp{\raggedright\tiny \raggedright\tiny \raggedright\tiny \raggedright\tiny \ref{lem:decompositions push forward} lem:decompositions push forward}\ignorespaces\fi
Suppose $t \colon X \rightarrow Y$ is a continuous function and $\lambda$ is a measure on $X$, and further suppose we have a family of measures $\lambda_y$ (for $y \in Y$) and a measure $\lambda'$ on $Y$ which are a decomposition of $\lambda$ with respect to $t$. 

Further, suppose that we have a Borel map $g \colon X \rightarrow Z$ and a map $s \colon Z \rightarrow Y$ so that $s \circ g = t$. Then the pushforwards $g_\sharp \lambda_y$ and the measure $\lambda'$ on $Y$ are a decomposition of $g_\sharp \lambda$ with respect to $s$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}[Proof of lemma]
Since the $y \mapsto \lambda_y$ is a continuous map from $y$ to Radon measures, and $\mu \mapsto g_\sharp \mu$ is a continuous map between measures, the composition $y \mapsto g_\sharp \lambda_y$ is continuous. 

Suppose we have some open set $U \in Z$ so that $U \cap s^{-1}(y) = \emptyset$. We claim that $g_\sharp \lambda_y (U) = 0$. We know that $g_\sharp \lambda_y (U) = \lambda_y (g^{-1}(U))$. We observe that $t(g^{-1}(U)) = s(g(g^{-1}(U))) \subset s(U)$. In particular, $y \not\in t(g^{-1}(U))$ since $y \notin s(U)$. Thus $\lambda_y (g^{-1}(U)) = 0$, as desired.

Suppose we have $f \in \mathcal{K}(Z)$. Then 
\begin{equation*}
g_\sharp \lambda(f) = \lambda (f \circ g) = \int \lambda_y(f \circ g) \lambda'(dy)
= \int (g_\sharp \lambda_y) (f) \lambda'(dy),
\end{equation*}
as desired.
\end{proof}
Now if we let $Q \colon \operatorname{ED} \rightarrow \operatorname{ED}$ and $\operatorname{proj}_{\operatorname{ID}} \colon \operatorname{ED} \rightarrow \operatorname{ID}$, we see that $Q^{-1} \circ \operatorname{proj}_{\operatorname{ID}}$ has the property that $Q \circ (Q^{-1} \circ \operatorname{proj}_{\operatorname{ID}}) = \operatorname{proj}_{\operatorname{ID}}$, and so by ~Lemma~\ref{lem:decompositions push forward}, the $Q_\# \mu^W_{\mathbf{G}}$ are a decomposition of $\mu$ with respect to $(Q^{-1} \circ \operatorname{proj}_{\operatorname{ID}})$, as desired.

It follows immediately that if we view $X$ as a $d \times \mathbf{v}$ matrix, the $d \times d$ matrix of expected dot products (in $\mathbb{R}^\mathbf{v}$) of coordinates of vertex positions $\operatorname{\mathcal{E}}_{\nu_{\mathbf{G}}}\! \left(XX^T\right) = (\operatorname{tr} \Sigma_\mathbf{v}) I_d$ and the $\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{v}$ matrix of expected dot products (in $\mathbb{R}^d$) of vertex vectors $\operatorname{\mathcal{E}}_{\nu_{\mathbf{G}}}\! \left(X^TX\right) = d \Sigma_\mathbf{v}$.

title: Proof
body_md:
As above, 
\begin{align*}
\operatorname{\mathcal{E}}_{\nu}\! \left(XX^T\right) &= \operatorname{\mathcal{E}}_{(Q \otimes I_\mathbf{v})_\sharp \nu}\! \left((Q \otimes I_\mathbf{v}) X X^T (Q^T \otimes I_\mathbf{v})\right) \\
&= \operatorname{\mathcal{E}}_{\nu}\! \left((Q \otimes I_\mathbf{v}) X X^T (Q^T \otimes I_\mathbf{v})\right) 
= (Q \otimes I_\mathbf{v}) \operatorname{\mathcal{E}}_{\nu}\! \left(X X^T\right) (Q^T \otimes I_\mathbf{v}).
\end{align*}
But if $\operatorname{\mathcal{E}}_{\nu}\! \left(X X^T\right)$ is invariant under conjugation by $Q \otimes I_\mathbf{v}$, as a $d \times d$ matrix of $\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{v}$ blocks, it must be\footnote{To expand on this point, first consider the diagonal matrix $Q \in O(d)$ with $(-1,1,\dots,1)$ on the diagonal. Conjugation by this $Q$ reverses the sign of all the blocks in the first column and first row except the block on the diagonal. Thus all these blocks (and by extension, all the off-diagonal blocks) must be zero matrices. Now consider the permutation matrix $Q \in O(d)$ which swaps $i$ and $j$. Conjugation by this matrix swaps the $i$-th and $j$-th diagonal blocks (and the $ij$ and $ji$ off-diagonal blocks) so the diagonal blocks must be equal.} blockwise a $d \times d$ scalar matrix, as scalar matrices are the only $d \times d$ matrices fixed by $O(d)$. 

Since $\operatorname{\mathcal{E}}_{\nu}\! \left(XX^T\right)$ is an average of symmetric positive semidefinite matrices $XX^T$, it is symmetric and positive semidefinite. Therefore, the $\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{v}$ diagonal block $\Sigma_\mathbf{v}$ is symmetric and positive semidefinite as well.

title: Proof
body_md:
It is clear that $\mu$ is an $O(d)$-invariant probability distribution as it's the joint distribution of $O(d)$-invariant random variables. Thus $\mu$ is admissible. Further, $\mu$ is permutation invariant on edges since the individual distributions are independent and identical. 

We have assumed that $\mu$ is compatible with $\mathbf{G}$, so $\mu_{\mathbf{G}}$ is well-defined. Permutation invariance of the conditional distribution $\mu_{\mathbf{G}}$ can be proved by uniqueness of decompositions as we did in the proof of $O(d)$-invariance in~Proposition~\ref{prop:disintegration}. 

Using this permutation symmetry, all of the off-diagonal elements of the $\mathbf{e} \times \mathbf{e}$ matrix $\operatorname{\mathcal{E}}_{\mu_{\mathbf{G}}}\! \left(W^T W\right)$ of edge covariances are equal, and all of the on-diagonal elements are equal as well. Since the loop space of the cycle graph $\ker \partial \in \operatorname{EC}$ is one-dimensional and spanned by $1_{\mathbf{e} \times 1}$, we know $1_{\mathbf{e} \times 1}$ spans $\ker \operatorname{\mathcal{E}}_{\mu_{\mathbf{G}}}\! \left(W^T W\right)$ and the sum of each row and column is zero. Thus
\begin{equation}
\operatorname{\mathcal{E}}_{\mu_{\mathbf{G}}}\! \left(W^T W\right) = \frac{\lambda \mathbf{e}}{\mathbf{e} - 1} I_\mathbf{e} - \frac{\lambda}{\mathbf{e}-1} \mathbf{1}_{\mathbf{e} \times \mathbf{e}}.
\end{equation}
where the diagonal element $\lambda$ is the expected squared norm of a single edge~\emph{in $\mu_{\mathbf{G}}$}. 

We have $\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{e}$ and $\partial$ is a (square) circulant matrix with first row $-1, 0, \dotsc, 0, 1$. It follows that $\partial^T \partial$ is a symmetric circulant matrix; its first row is $2, -1, \dots, 0, -1$. Since the row and column sums of $\partial^T \partial$ vanish, the row and column sums of $(\partial^T \partial)^+$ vanish as well and $\mathbf{1}_{\mathbf{e} \times \mathbf{e}} (\partial^T \partial)^+ = 0$. Further, the trace of $\partial^T \partial$ is\footnote{Eigenvalues of a circulant are well-known; to sum them use $\sum_{j=1}^{v-1} \csc^2 (\pi j)=(1/3)(v^2-1)$~\cite[4.4.6.5, p.\ 644]{Prudnikov:1986vp}.} $\frac{1}{12} (\mathbf{e}^2-1)$. 

Now we are ready to compute. Since $\mu_{\mathbf{G}}$ is (by construction) $O(d)$-invariant and concentrated on $\operatorname{im} \partial^*$,~Theorem~\ref{thm:gyradius formula} applies. Rearranging it and using $d \Sigma_\mathbf{e} = \operatorname{\mathcal{E}}_{\mu_{\mathbf{G}}}\! \left(W^T W\right)$,
\begin{align*}
\left< \operatorname{R^2_g} \right> = \frac{1}{\mathbf{e}} \operatorname{tr} \left(\operatorname{\mathcal{E}}_{\mu_{\mathbf{G}}}\! \left(W^T W\right) (\partial^T \partial)^+ \right)
 	      = \frac{1}{\mathbf{e}} \operatorname{tr} \left(\lambda \frac{\mathbf{e}}{\mathbf{e}-1} (\partial^T \partial)^+ \right) 
	      = \frac{\lambda (\mathbf{e} + 1)}{12}.
\end{align*}

Then $\mu'$ is compatible with $\mathbf{G}'$ and 
the corresponding $\nu_{\mathbf{G}} := \partial^{*+}_\sharp \mu_{\mathbf{G}}$ and $\nu'_{\mathbf{G}'} := (\partial')^{*+}_\sharp (\mu')_{\mathbf{G}'}$ measures are related by
\begin{equation*}
(\operatorname{proj}_{\operatorname{im} (\partial')^{*+}} f_0^*)_\sharp \nu_{\mathbf{G}} = \nu'_{\mathbf{G}'}.
\end{equation*}
It follows that if $g$ is any $O(d)$ and translation-invariant function $g \colon \operatorname{VP} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ which is expressed in terms of $\mathbf{G}'$, we have $\operatorname{\mathcal{E}}_{\nu_{\mathbf{G}}}\! \left(g\right) = \operatorname{\mathcal{E}}_{\nu'_{\mathbf{G}'}}\! \left(g'\right)$.

The $n$-part edge subdivision $\mathbf{G}_n$ of a multigraph $\mathbf{G}$ is the graph obtained by dividing each edge of $\mathbf{G}$ into $n$ smaller edges (see Figure~\ref{fig:subdivisions}) oriented to agree with the original graph.

If $\mathbf{G}$ has $\mathbf{v}$ vertices $v_1, \dotsc, v_{\mathbf{v}}$  then $\mathbf{G}_n$ has $\mathbf{v}$~\emph{junction vertices} $v_{1 0}, \dotsc, v_{\mathbf{v} 0}$ corresponding to the vertices of $\mathbf{G}$ and $(n-1) \mathbf{e}$ \emph{subdivision vertices} $v_{11}, \dotsc, v_{1(n-1)}, v_{21}, \dotsc, v_{\mathbf{e} (n-1)}$ located along the subdivided edges.

If $\mathbf{G}$ has $\mathbf{e}$ edges $e_1, \dotsc, e_{\mathbf{e}}$, then $\mathbf{G}_n$ has $n\mathbf{e}$ edges $e_{11}, \dotsc, e_{1n}, e_{21}, \dotsc, e_{\mathbf{e} n}$. We will call each group $e_{j1}, \dotsc, e_{jn}$ the~\emph{subdivided edge} corresponding to $e_j$ in $\mathbf{G}$. 

There are canonical chain maps $f_0(v_i) = v_{i0}$ and $f_1(e_j) = e_{j1} + \cdots + e_{jn}$ from $\mathbf{G}$ to $\mathbf{G}_n$ which take vertices of $\mathbf{G}$ to the corresponding junction vertices in $\mathbf{G}_n$ and edges of $\mathbf{G}$ to the corresponding subdivided edges in $\mathbf{G}_n$.

We will reserve our usual notations $\mu, \mu_{\mathbf{G}}, \partial, \operatorname{EC}, \operatorname{VC}, \operatorname{VP}, \operatorname{ED}$ to refer to $\mathbf{G}$ and use the notations $\mu_n, \mu_{\mathbf{G}_n}, \partial_n, \operatorname{EC}_n, \operatorname{VC}_n, \operatorname{VP}_n, \operatorname{ED}_n$ for the corresponding objects for the subdivided graph $\mathbf{G}_n$.

\label{lem:adjoint formula}\ifinner\else\mgp{\raggedright\tiny \ref{lem:adjoint formula} lem:adjoint formula}\ignorespaces\fi\ifinner\else\mgp{\raggedright\tiny \raggedright\tiny \ref{lem:adjoint formula} lem:adjoint formula}\ignorespaces\fi\ifinner\else\mgp{\raggedright\tiny \raggedright\tiny \raggedright\tiny \ref{lem:adjoint formula} lem:adjoint formula}\ignorespaces\fi\ifinner\else\mgp{\raggedright\tiny \raggedright\tiny \raggedright\tiny \raggedright\tiny \ref{lem:adjoint formula} lem:adjoint formula}\ignorespaces\fi
	Suppose $V$ and $W$ are finite-dimensional vector spaces with bases $v_1, \dots , v_n$ and $w_1, \dots, w_m$, respectively, and corresponding standard inner products $\left< -, - \right>_{V,\operatorname{std}}$ and $\left< -, - \right>_{W,\operatorname{std}}$. Suppose $F \colon V \to V$ and $H \colon W \to W$ are positive-definite and self-adjoint with respect to the standard inner products. If $A \colon V \to W$ is linear, then the adjoint of $A$ with respect to the $\left< -, - \right>_{V,F}$ and $\left< -, - \right>_{W,H}$ inner products is represented by the matrix
	\[
		A^\dag = F^{-1} A^T H.
	\]

label: eq:theta adjoint
title: Proof
body_md:
By definition of the adjoint,
		\begin{equation}\label{eq:theta adjoint}\ifinner\else\mgp{\raggedright\tiny \ref{eq:theta adjoint} eq:theta adjoint}\ignorespaces\fi\ifinner\else\mgp{\raggedright\tiny \raggedright\tiny \ref{eq:theta adjoint} eq:theta adjoint}\ignorespaces\fi\ifinner\else\mgp{\raggedright\tiny \raggedright\tiny \raggedright\tiny \ref{eq:theta adjoint} eq:theta adjoint}\ignorespaces\fi\ifinner\else\mgp{\raggedright\tiny \raggedright\tiny \raggedright\tiny \raggedright\tiny \ref{eq:theta adjoint} eq:theta adjoint}\ignorespaces\fi
			\left< A v, w \right>_{W,H} = \left< v, A^\dag w \right>_{V,F}
		\end{equation}
		for any $v \in V$ and $w \in W$. In turn, the left hand side is equal to
		\[
			\left< A v, H w \right>_{W,\operatorname{std}} = \left< v, A^T H w \right>_{V,\operatorname{std}}
		\]
		and the right hand side is equal to
		\[
			\left< v, F A^\dag w \right>_{V,\operatorname{std}}.                                             
		\]
		Equating these two and recalling that equation~\eqref{eq:theta adjoint} must hold for all $v$ and $w$, we conclude that $A^T H  = F A^\dag$ or, since $F$ is invertible,
		\[
			A^\dag = F^{-1} A^T H.
		\]

\label{prop:hom inner product}\ifinner\else\mgp{\raggedright\tiny \ref{prop:hom inner product} prop:hom inner product}\ignorespaces\fi\ifinner\else\mgp{\raggedright\tiny \raggedright\tiny \ref{prop:hom inner product} prop:hom inner product}\ignorespaces\fi\ifinner\else\mgp{\raggedright\tiny \raggedright\tiny \raggedright\tiny \ref{prop:hom inner product} prop:hom inner product}\ignorespaces\fi\ifinner\else\mgp{\raggedright\tiny \raggedright\tiny \raggedright\tiny \raggedright\tiny \ref{prop:hom inner product} prop:hom inner product}\ignorespaces\fi
	Under the same hypotheses as in Lemma~\ref{lem:adjoint formula}, the Frobenius inner product on $\operatorname{Hom}(V,W)$ induced by $\left< -, - \right>_{V,F}$ and $\left< -, - \right>_{W,H}$ is
	\[
		\left< -, - \right>_{\operatorname{Fr}} = \left< -, - \right>_{H \otimes F^{-1}}
	\]

If $Fu = v$, then $\widehat{u} = F^+ v$ minimizes $\left\| Fu -v  \right\|_{V}^2 = \left< Fu-v, Fu-v \right>_{V}$. Further, $F F^+$ is orthogonal projection (with respect to $\left< -, - \right>_{V}$) onto $\operatorname{im} F$, while $F^+ F$ is orthogonal projection (with respect to $\left< -, - \right>_{U}$) onto $\operatorname{im} F^\dag$. In addition, $\ker F^+ = \ker F^\dag$ and $\operatorname{im} F^+ = \operatorname{im} F^\dag$. Further, $(F^\dag)^+ = (F^+)^\dag$ so we can write $F^{\dag +}$ without ambiguity.

body_md:
\label{prop:starplus is plusstar}\ifinner\else\mgp{\raggedright\tiny \ref{prop:starplus is plusstar} prop:starplus is plusstar}\ignorespaces\fi\ifinner\else\mgp{\raggedright\tiny \raggedright\tiny \ref{prop:starplus is plusstar} prop:starplus is plusstar}\ignorespaces\fi\ifinner\else\mgp{\raggedright\tiny \raggedright\tiny \raggedright\tiny \ref{prop:starplus is plusstar} prop:starplus is plusstar}\ignorespaces\fi\ifinner\else\mgp{\raggedright\tiny \raggedright\tiny \raggedright\tiny \raggedright\tiny \ref{prop:starplus is plusstar} prop:starplus is plusstar}\ignorespaces\fi
Suppose we have inner product spaces $\left( U, \left< -, - \right>_{U} \right)$, $\left( V, \left< -, - \right>_{V} \right)$, and $\left( W, \left< -, - \right>_{W} \right)$, together with $\operatorname{Hom}(U,W)$ and $\operatorname{Hom}(V,W)$ with their induced (Frobenius) inner products, and a linear map $F \colon U \rightarrow V$. Then $(F^*)^+ = (F^+)^*$. Both are maps $\operatorname{Hom}(U,W) \rightarrow \operatorname{Hom}(V,W)$.
